Orionis Analytics Ltd.        14 Fitzwilliam Square East, Dublin 2, D02 W526, Ireland               Dublin, Ireland              Anonymization and analytics services

**6.3** The Processor shall inform the Controller of any intended changes concerning the addition or replacement of Subprocessors, thereby giving the Controller the opportunity to object to such changes in accordance with this Section 6. The Processor shall provide written notice to the Controller at least fifteen (15) calendar days prior to the engagement of any new Subprocessor or the replacement of an existing Subprocessor. Such notice shall identify the proposed Subprocessor, its location, the Processing activities to be performed, and the measures taken to ensure compliance with Applicable Data Protection Law.

**6.4** If the Controller raises a reasonable objection to a proposed new or replacement Subprocessor within the fifteen (15) calendar day notice period set forth in Section 6.3, the Parties shall discuss the Controller\'s concerns in good faith with a view to reaching a mutually acceptable resolution. If the Parties are unable to resolve the Controller\'s objection within thirty (30) calendar days following the Controller\'s written objection, the Controller may terminate the affected Services (i.e., those Services that would require the use of the objected-to Subprocessor) without penalty upon sixty (60) days\' written notice to the Processor. The Processor shall not engage the objected-to Subprocessor for the affected Services during any ongoing objection or termination period.

**6.5** The Processor shall impose on each Subprocessor, by way of a written contract, data protection obligations that are equivalent to those set out in this DPA, in particular providing sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures in such a manner that the Processing carried out by the Subprocessor will meet the requirements of the GDPR. The Processor shall ensure that each subprocessing agreement includes, at a minimum, the obligations set forth in Article 28(3) of the GDPR, including the obligation to Process Personal Data only on documented instructions, to ensure the confidentiality of personnel, to implement appropriate security measures, and to assist the Controller with data subject requests and breach notifications.

**6.6** The Processor shall remain fully liable to the Controller for the performance of each Subprocessor\'s obligations under this DPA and the applicable subprocessing agreement. Where a Subprocessor fails to fulfil its data protection obligations, the Processor shall remain fully liable to the Controller for the Subprocessor\'s failure as if the Processor itself had performed the relevant Processing activities.
**[SECTION 7 --- INTERNATIONAL DATA TRANSFERS]{.underline}**

**7.1** The Processor shall not transfer Personal Data to any country or territory outside the European Economic Area (\"EEA\") or to any international organization, and shall not permit any Subprocessor to make any such transfer, unless one of the following conditions is satisfied:

> \(a\) The European Commission has issued an adequacy decision for the recipient country, territory, or international organization, or a specified sector within such country, pursuant to Article 45 of the GDPR, and such adequacy decision remains in force and has not been invalidated by the Court of Justice of the European Union or otherwise;

> \(b\) Appropriate safeguards have been provided in accordance with Article 46 of the GDPR, including but not limited to the execution of Standard Contractual Clauses approved by the European Commission, the adoption of binding corporate rules approved by a competent Supervisory Authority, or the use of an approved certification mechanism together with binding and enforceable commitments of the data importer; or

> \(c\) A derogation for specific situations under Article 49 of the GDPR applies, provided that such derogation is interpreted restrictively in accordance with the guidance of the European Data Protection Board.

**7.2** To the extent that the Processing involves transfers of Personal Data from the EEA to the United States of America or to any other third country that is not subject to an adequacy decision by the European Commission, the Parties hereby agree to enter into the Standard Contractual Clauses as set forth in Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of 4 June 2021 on standard contractual clauses for the transfer of personal data to third countries pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council. The applicable Standard Contractual Clauses are Module 2 (Transfer Controller to Processor), and such SCCs are incorporated by reference into this DPA as if set forth herein in full. The completed Annexes to the Standard Contractual Clauses, including the description of the transfer, the technical and organizational measures, and the list of Subprocessors, are set forth in Annex A to this DPA. In the event of any conflict between the Standard Contractual Clauses and any other provision of this DPA, the Standard Contractual Clauses shall prevail to the extent of the conflict.

**7.3** The Processor shall cooperate with the Controller in good faith to ensure that appropriate and legally sufficient safeguards are in place for any international transfer of Personal Data carried out in connection with the Services, including any transfers that may arise from changes in applicable law, regulatory guidance, or judicial decisions affecting the validity or adequacy of existing transfer mechanisms. The Processor shall promptly inform the Controller if, in the Processor\'s reasonable opinion, any existing transfer safeguard is or may become insufficient to ensure lawful transfers under Applicable Data Protection Law.
**[SECTION 8 --- DATA SUBJECT RIGHTS]{.underline}**

**8.1** The Processor shall, taking into account the nature of the Processing, assist the Controller by appropriate technical and organizational measures, insofar as this is possible, for the fulfilment of the Controller\'s obligation to respond to requests for exercising the rights of Data Subjects under Chapter III of the GDPR (Articles 15 through 22). Such Data Subject rights include, without limitation:
> \(a\) The right of access (Article 15 GDPR);
> \(b\) The right to rectification (Article 16 GDPR);
> \(c\) The right to erasure (\"right to be forgotten\") (Article 17 GDPR);
> \(d\) The right to restriction of processing (Article 18 GDPR);
> \(e\) The notification obligation regarding rectification, erasure, or restriction (Article 19 GDPR);
> \(f\) The right to data portability (Article 20 GDPR);
> \(g\) The right to object (Article 21 GDPR); and
> \(h\) The right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling (Article 22 GDPR).

**8.2** The Processor shall promptly, and in any event within five (5) business days, notify the Controller if the Processor receives a request from a Data Subject directly in relation to the Controller\'s Personal Data. The Processor shall not respond to any such Data Subject request itself unless expressly authorized in writing by the Controller to do so. The Processor shall provide the Controller with a copy of the Data Subject request and any information reasonably necessary to assist the Controller in evaluating and responding to the request.

**8.3** The Processor shall provide substantive assistance to the Controller in responding to Data Subject requests within ten (10) business days of the Controller\'s written request for such assistance. Such assistance may include, as applicable, searching the Processor\'s systems for the relevant Personal Data, providing copies of Personal Data in a commonly used, machine-readable format, implementing restrictions on Processing, or effecting the erasure of Personal Data from the Processor\'s systems. The Controller acknowledges that the Processor\'s ability to assist may depend on the nature of the Services and the architecture of the Processor\'s systems.

**8.4** To the extent that the Processor incurs material costs in providing assistance under this Section 8 beyond what is reasonably anticipated in the ordinary course of the Services, the Processor may charge the Controller reasonable fees for such assistance, based on the Processor\'s then-current professional services rates, provided that the Processor has obtained the Controller\'s prior written approval for any such charges.
**[SECTION 9 --- PERSONAL DATA BREACH NOTIFICATION]{.underline}**

**9.1** The Processor shall notify the Controller of any Personal Data Breach without undue delay and in any event no later than forty-eight (48) hours after becoming aware of the Personal Data Breach. For the purposes of this Section 9, the Processor shall be deemed to have become \"aware\" of a Personal Data Breach when the Processor\'s incident response team or any member of the Processor\'s management has confirmed, following initial assessment, that a security incident constitutes a Personal Data Breach within the meaning of Article 4(12) of the GDPR. The Processor shall maintain documented procedures to ensure that potential Personal Data Breaches are identified, escalated, and assessed promptly.

**9.2** The notification provided under Section 9.1 shall include, to the extent such information is available at the time of notification and to the extent it can be provided without unreasonable delay:

> \(a\) A description of the nature of the Personal Data Breach, including, where possible, the categories and approximate number of Data Subjects concerned and the categories and approximate number of Personal Data records concerned;

> \(b\) The name and contact details of the Processor\'s Data Protection Officer (or, if the Data Protection Officer is unavailable, another designated contact point) where more information can be obtained regarding the Personal Data Breach;
> \(c\) A description of the likely consequences of the Personal Data Breach, including an assessment of the potential risks to the rights and freedoms of affected Data Subjects;

> \(d\) A description of the measures taken or proposed to be taken by the Processor to address the Personal Data Breach, including, where appropriate, measures to contain the breach, mitigate its possible adverse effects, and prevent recurrence.

**9.3** Where, and to the extent that, it is not possible to provide all of the information specified in Section 9.2 at the same time as the initial notification, the Processor shall provide such information in phases without undue further delay as additional information becomes available. The Processor shall provide supplemental notifications to the Controller as soon as reasonably practicable and in any event shall endeavor to provide complete information within seventy-two (72) hours of the initial notification.

**9.4** The Processor shall document all Personal Data Breaches, including the facts relating to the Personal Data Breach, its effects, and the remedial action taken, in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. Such documentation shall be maintained for a period of not less than three (3) years from the date of the Personal Data Breach and shall be made available to the Controller upon request.

**9.5** The Processor shall cooperate with and assist the Controller in the Controller\'s performance of its obligations under Articles 33 and 34 of the GDPR, including the Controller\'s obligation to notify the competent Supervisory Authority and, where applicable, to communicate the Personal Data Breach to affected Data Subjects. The Processor shall provide such cooperation and assistance promptly and in a manner that enables the Controller to meet the applicable notification timelines under the GDPR.

**9.6** In the event that the Processor fails to provide the initial notification of a Personal Data Breach within the forty-eight (48) hour timeline specified in Section 9.1, the Processor shall pay to the Controller a penalty of one thousand Euros (€1,000) per calendar day of delay commencing on the date that is forty-eight (48) hours after the Processor became aware of the Personal Data Breach and continuing until the date on which notification is actually provided to the Controller, provided that such penalty shall not exceed fifty thousand Euros (€50,000) in the aggregate per breach incident. The Parties acknowledge that such penalties represent a genuine pre-estimate of the Controller\'s loss resulting from delayed notification and are not intended as punitive damages.

**9.7** The obligations set forth in this Section 9 are without prejudice to any other rights, remedies, or claims the Controller may have under this DPA, the Agreement, or applicable law in connection with a Personal Data Breach.
**[SECTION 10 --- DATA PROTECTION IMPACT ASSESSMENTS]{.underline}**

**10.1** The Processor shall provide reasonable assistance to the Controller in the conduct of data protection impact assessments (\"DPIAs\") pursuant to Article 35 of the GDPR, where the Controller determines that a type of Processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. The Processor shall also provide reasonable assistance to the Controller in connection with prior consultations with the competent Supervisory Authority pursuant to Article 36 of the GDPR, where the results of a DPIA indicate that the Processing would result in a high risk in the absence of measures taken by the Controller to mitigate the risk. In each case, the Processor\'s obligation to provide assistance shall take into account the nature of the Processing activities and the information available to the Processor.

**10.2** Such assistance shall include, without limitation, providing the Controller with information regarding the Processor\'s technical and organizational measures as described in Annex B, the Processing activities carried out on behalf of the Controller as described in Annex A, the results of any security assessments, penetration tests, or audits conducted by or on behalf of the Processor, and such other information as is reasonably necessary for the Controller to conduct a comprehensive DPIA. The Processor shall respond to the Controller\'s reasonable requests for information in connection with a DPIA within a reasonable timeframe, and in any event within twenty (20) business days of the Controller\'s request.

**10.3** The Processor may charge reasonable fees for assistance provided under this Section 10, based on the Processor\'s then-current professional services rates and the scope and complexity of the assistance requested. The Processor shall provide the Controller with a fee estimate prior to commencing any such assistance and shall obtain the Controller\'s written approval before incurring fees in excess of five thousand Euros (€5,000) for any single DPIA engagement.
**[SECTION 11 --- AUDIT RIGHTS]{.underline}**

**11.1** The Processor shall make available to the Controller all information necessary to demonstrate compliance with the obligations laid down in Article 28 of the GDPR and this DPA, and shall allow for and contribute to audits, including inspections, conducted by the Controller or another auditor mandated by the Controller, in accordance with Article 28(3)(h) of the GDPR. The Processor shall cooperate in good faith with the Controller in connection with any such audit and shall provide the Controller\'s audit team with reasonable access to relevant documentation, systems, and personnel.

**11.2** The Controller may conduct an audit of the Processor\'s Processing activities no more than once per calendar year, subject to at least thirty (30) calendar days\' prior written notice to the Processor. Audits shall be conducted during the Processor\'s normal business hours (Monday through Friday, 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Central European Time, excluding German public holidays) and shall not unreasonably interfere with the Processor\'s business operations or the Processor\'s obligations to its other customers. The Controller\'s audit team shall comply with the Processor\'s reasonable security and confidentiality requirements while on the Processor\'s premises.

**11.3** Audits conducted under Section 11.2 shall be limited to the Processor\'s primary data processing facility located in Frankfurt, Germany. The scope of each audit shall be limited to the Processing activities performed by the Processor on behalf of the Controller and shall not extend to the confidential information of the Processor\'s other customers or to systems that do not Process the Controller\'s Personal Data.
**11.4** The Processor may, at its sole discretion, satisfy the Controller\'s audit requests in whole or in part by providing the Controller with one or more of the following:

> \(a\) A current SOC 2 Type II report prepared by Clearwater Audit Partners GmbH (or a successor firm that is a nationally or internationally recognized independent audit firm) covering the Processor\'s controls relevant to the Services provided to the Controller; and/or

> \(b\) A current ISO 27001 certification report or certificate issued by an accredited certification body, demonstrating the Processor\'s compliance with ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or its successor standard.

**11.5** For reference, the most recent SOC 2 Type II report available as of the date of this DPA was dated September 30, 2024, covering the audit period from October 1, 2023 through September 30, 2024, and was issued by Clearwater Audit Partners GmbH. The Processor shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain an updated SOC 2 Type II report on an annual basis and shall make the most recent report available to the Controller within thirty (30) calendar days of the Controller\'s written request.

**11.6** The Controller shall bear all costs and expenses associated with any audit conducted under this Section 11, including without limitation travel, accommodation, and professional fees for the Controller\'s audit team or mandated auditors, unless the audit reveals a material breach of this DPA by the Processor, in which case the Processor shall reimburse the Controller for the reasonable and documented costs of the audit, up to a maximum of twenty-five thousand Euros (€25,000) per audit.
**[SECTION 12 --- DATA DELETION]{.underline}**

**12.1** Upon termination or expiration of the Agreement for any reason, the Processor shall, at the Controller\'s choice and subject to Section 12.2, delete all Personal Data Processed on behalf of the Controller, including all copies, backups, and archives thereof, within ninety (90) calendar days of the effective date of termination or expiration of the Agreement. Deletion shall be performed using industry-standard secure deletion methods that render the Personal Data unrecoverable, including, where applicable, cryptographic erasure, multi-pass overwriting, or physical destruction of storage media.

**12.2** Notwithstanding Section 12.1, the Processor may retain Personal Data to the extent and for the duration required by European Union or German federal or state law to which the Processor is subject, including without limitation any mandatory data retention obligations under German commercial law (*Handelsgesetzbuch*) or German tax law (*Abgabenordnung*). In such cases, the Processor shall promptly inform the Controller of the applicable legal requirement and the categories of Personal Data to be retained, and shall limit its Processing of the retained Personal Data strictly to the purposes required by such law. The Processor shall ensure that retained Personal Data is subject to the confidentiality and security obligations set forth in this DPA for the duration of its retention.

**12.3** Upon request by the Controller following the completion of deletion under Section 12.1, the Processor shall provide written confirmation of the deletion of the Controller\'s Personal Data, signed by an authorized officer of the Processor. Such confirmation shall specify the date of deletion, the categories of data deleted, and the deletion methods used. The Processor shall provide such confirmation within thirty (30) calendar days of the Controller\'s request.

**12.4** The Controller acknowledges that deletion of Personal Data from the Processor\'s backup systems may require additional time beyond the ninety (90) calendar day period specified in Section 12.1 due to the Processor\'s automated backup rotation cycles. In such cases, the Processor shall ensure that all Personal Data is deleted from backup systems within one hundred eighty (180) calendar days of the effective date of termination or expiration, and shall isolate and restrict access to such backup copies pending their deletion.
**[SECTION 13 --- LIABILITY]{.underline}**

**13.1** The Processor\'s aggregate liability for all claims of any kind arising under or in connection with this DPA, whether in contract, tort (including negligence), strict liability, or otherwise, shall not exceed five hundred thousand Euros (€500,000). This limitation applies to the aggregate of all claims arising under or in connection with this DPA, regardless of the number of events, incidents, or claims giving rise to such liability.

**13.2** In no event shall the Processor be liable for any indirect, incidental, consequential, special, punitive, or exemplary damages arising out of or related to this DPA, including but not limited to loss of revenue, loss of profits, loss of business or anticipated savings, loss of goodwill, loss of data or corruption of data, or cost of procurement of substitute services, regardless of the theory of liability and even if the Processor has been advised of the possibility of such damages or should have foreseen the possibility thereof. This exclusion of consequential damages shall apply to the maximum extent permitted by applicable law.

**13.3** The limitations and exclusions set forth in this Section 13 shall apply to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law and shall survive the termination or expiration of this DPA. The Parties acknowledge that the limitations and exclusions set forth in this Section 13 reflect a fair and reasonable allocation of risk between the Parties, taking into account the nature of the Services, the fees payable under the Agreement, and the respective responsibilities of the Parties under this DPA and applicable law.

**13.4** Nothing in this Section 13 shall limit the Processor\'s liability for damages caused by a failure to comply with its obligations under the GDPR specifically directed to processors, or for damages caused to Data Subjects arising from the Processor\'s non-compliance with its obligations under Article 82 of the GDPR. Article 82 of the GDPR provides that any processor involved in processing shall be liable for damage caused by processing only where it has not complied with obligations of the GDPR specifically directed to processors, or where it has acted outside of or contrary to lawful instructions of the controller.

**13.5** For the avoidance of doubt, each Party shall be liable for the entirety of the damage suffered by a Data Subject in accordance with Article 82(4) of the GDPR, subject to any right of recourse between the Parties as provided in Article 82(5) of the GDPR. Where a Party has paid full compensation for the damage suffered, that Party shall be entitled to claim back from the other Party that part of the compensation corresponding to the other Party\'s share of responsibility for the damage.
**[SECTION 14 --- GOVERNING LAW AND DISPUTE RESOLUTION]{.underline}**

**14.1** This DPA and any disputes arising out of or in connection with this DPA, including disputes regarding the existence, validity, interpretation, performance, breach, or termination of this DPA, and including any non-contractual claims arising out of or in connection with this DPA, shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the Federal Republic of Germany, without regard to its conflict of laws principles that would result in the application of the laws of any other jurisdiction. To the extent that the GDPR or other mandatory provisions of European Union law apply to any matter arising under this DPA, such provisions shall prevail over any inconsistent provisions of German national law.

**14.2** Any dispute arising out of or in connection with this DPA that the Parties are unable to resolve through good-faith negotiations within thirty (30) calendar days of one Party\'s written notice to the other Party describing the nature of the dispute and the relief sought, shall be finally settled by arbitration administered by the Deutsche Institution für Schiedsgerichtsbarkeit e.V. (\"DIS\") in accordance with the DIS Arbitration Rules (DIS-Schiedsgerichtsordnung) in effect at the time of the commencement of the arbitration proceedings. The seat of arbitration shall be Munich, Germany. The language of the arbitration proceedings shall be English. The arbitral tribunal shall consist of three (3) arbitrators, with each Party nominating one arbitrator and the two Party-nominated arbitrators selecting the presiding arbitrator. If the two Party-nominated arbitrators fail to agree on the selection of the presiding arbitrator within thirty (30) calendar days of the appointment of the second Party-nominated arbitrator, the presiding arbitrator shall be appointed by the DIS Appointing Authority in accordance with the DIS Arbitration Rules.

**14.3** The arbitral tribunal shall have the authority to award any remedy or relief that a court of competent jurisdiction could grant, including but not limited to monetary damages, declaratory relief, and specific performance, provided that the arbitral tribunal shall not have the authority to award punitive or exemplary damages except to the extent that such damages are recoverable under Article 82 of the GDPR or other mandatory provisions of applicable law.

**14.4** Nothing in this Section 14 shall prevent either Party from seeking interim, provisional, or injunctive relief from any court of competent jurisdiction, including courts in Germany or any other jurisdiction, where such relief is necessary to prevent irreparable harm or to preserve the status quo pending the resolution of a dispute through arbitration. Any application for interim or injunctive relief shall not be deemed a waiver of the right to arbitrate.

**14.5** All arbitration proceedings and any arbitral award shall be kept strictly confidential by the Parties and the arbitrators, except to the extent that disclosure is required by applicable law, by a Supervisory Authority, or in connection with the enforcement of an arbitral award.
**[SECTION 15 --- DATA PROTECTION OFFICER]{.underline}**

**15.1** The Processor has appointed a Data Protection Officer in accordance with Articles 37 through 39 of the GDPR. As of the date of this DPA, the Processor\'s designated Data Protection Officer is:
> **Dr. Annika Vogt** Data Protection Officer Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH Hohenzollernstraße 88 80796 Munich, Germany
> Email: dpo@stratospherecloud.example.com

**15.2** The Controller may direct data protection inquiries, requests, or complaints related to the Processing of Personal Data under this DPA to the Processor\'s Data Protection Officer at the contact details set forth above. The Processor shall ensure that the Data Protection Officer is available to respond to the Controller\'s inquiries within a reasonable timeframe and, in any event, within ten (10) business days of receipt of a written inquiry.

**15.3** The Processor shall promptly notify the Controller in writing of any change in the identity or contact details of its Data Protection Officer, and in any event within fifteen (15) calendar days of such change.
**[SECTION 16 --- TERM AND SURVIVAL]{.underline}**

**16.1** This DPA shall become effective on the date of its execution by both Parties (the \"Effective Date\") and shall remain in full force and effect for the duration of the Agreement, including any renewals, extensions, or amendments thereof, for so long as the Processor Processes Personal Data on behalf of the Controller.

**16.2** This DPA shall automatically terminate upon the termination or expiration of the Agreement, subject to the survival provisions set forth in Section 16.3 below and the Processor\'s obligations under Section 12 (Data Deletion).

**16.3** Notwithstanding the termination or expiration of this DPA, the following provisions shall survive and remain in full force and effect for a period of two (2) years following the effective date of termination or expiration:
> \(a\) Section 9 (Personal Data Breach Notification), to the extent the Processor discovers a Personal Data Breach relating to the Controller\'s Personal Data during the survival period;
> \(b\) Section 11 (Audit Rights), to the extent necessary for the Controller to verify the Processor\'s compliance with its post-termination obligations, including its obligations under Section 12;
> \(c\) Section 12 (Data Deletion), including the Processor\'s obligation to delete Personal Data and to provide written confirmation of such deletion;
> \(d\) Section 13 (Liability), with respect to any claims arising under or in connection with this DPA, whether such claims accrue before, on, or after the date of termination or expiration.

**16.4** The survival period specified in Section 16.3 shall commence on the effective date of termination or expiration of this DPA. Upon the expiration of the survival period, the surviving provisions shall cease to have effect, except to the extent that applicable law requires continued compliance with any obligation set forth therein.
**16.5** The provisions of Section 4 (Confidentiality) shall survive the termination or expiration of this DPA indefinitely in accordance with Section 4.3.
**[SECTION 17 --- GENERAL PROVISIONS]{.underline}**

**17.1 Entire Agreement.** This DPA, together with its Annexes and the Agreement, constitutes the entire agreement between the Parties with respect to the subject matter hereof and supersedes all prior and contemporaneous agreements, understandings, negotiations, and discussions, whether oral or written, between the Parties relating to the Processing of Personal Data in connection with the Services.

**17.2 Amendments.** No amendment, modification, or supplement to this DPA shall be effective unless it is in writing and signed by authorized representatives of both Parties. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the Processor may update Annex B (Technical and Organizational Measures) from time to time in accordance with Section 5.5 of this DPA.

401: > **(g) Notification of Inability to Comply.** Vendor must notify Pinnacle promptly if vendor determines that it can no longer meet its obligations under the CCPA/CPRA. Upon receipt of such notification, Pinnacle shall have the right to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate the unauthorized use of personal information, up to and including termination of the DPA/MSA.
402: 
403: **Nice-to-have:** Vendor agrees to cooperate with Pinnacle in responding to CCPA/CPRA consumer requests, including the right to know (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.110), the right to delete (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.105), the right to correct (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.106), and the right to opt-out of sale/sharing (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.120), within timelines consistent with the statute. Under the CCPA/CPRA, Pinnacle must respond to consumer requests within **forty-five (45) days**, with a **forty-five (45) day extension** upon notice to the consumer. Vendor\'s cooperation must be sufficiently prompt to allow Pinnacle to meet these deadlines.
404: 
405: **Fallback:** If the vendor\'s DPA template contains no CCPA/CPRA provisions whatsoever, Pinnacle will require a **standalone CCPA/CPRA Addendum** appended to the DPA. The addendum must contain all of the provisions listed in subparagraphs (a) through (g) above and must be expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference. The negotiator should use the template language provided in Appendix B as a starting point for drafting the addendum.
406: 
407: **[7.2 California Consumer Volume]{.underline}**
408: 
409: As of February 2025, Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents** across its patient platform, provider network, and associated data processing activities. This volume is expected to grow as Pinnacle\'s US user base expands. All vendors with access to California resident personal information, regardless of the volume of records processed by any individual vendor, must comply with the requirements set forth in Section 7.1 above.
410: 
411: **[Section 8: Audit Rights]{.underline}**
412: 
413: Audit provisions are a cornerstone of any effective DPA. Pinnacle\'s ability to verify vendor compliance with HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR depends on having contractual audit rights that are robust enough to cover all data processing locations, including subprocessor facilities, and all relevant compliance domains. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s audit right requirements.
414: 
415: **[8.1 Scope of Audit Rights]{.underline}**
416: 
417: **Must-have:** Pinnacle must have the contractual right to audit vendor\'s data processing activities, directly or through a qualified third-party auditor designated by Pinnacle. The scope of the audit right must include:
418: 
419: > **(a) All data center locations** where Pinnacle data is stored or processed. Audit rights must not be limited to the vendor\'s primary data center; they must extend to all locations, including secondary, disaster recovery, and backup sites.
420: >
421: > **(b) All subprocessor facilities** where Pinnacle data is stored or processed. This requirement is critical where subprocessors operate in different jurisdictions from the vendor (e.g., a US subprocessor handling EU data under a Processor-to-Subprocessor transfer). Subprocessor audit coverage is essential to verifying end-to-end compliance with the data protection requirements applicable to Pinnacle\'s data.
422: >
423: > **(c) Vendor\'s policies, procedures, and technical controls** relevant to data protection, including but not limited to: information security policies, access control procedures, incident response plans, data classification policies, encryption configurations, and vulnerability management programs.
424: >
425: > **(d) Vendor\'s compliance with HIPAA Security Rule safeguards** specifically, including administrative safeguards (45 CFR § 164.308), physical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.310), and technical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.312), where vendor is a Business Associate.
426: 
427: **Must-have:** Audit rights must extend to subprocessor locations. Vendor must provide Pinnacle with one of the following mechanisms for subprocessor audit coverage:
428: 
429: > \(i\) Vendor grants Pinnacle **direct audit rights** over subprocessor facilities, with the same scope and frequency as Pinnacle\'s audit rights over vendor; or
430: >
431: > \(ii\) Vendor **contractually requires** each subprocessor to submit to audits by Pinnacle or Pinnacle\'s designated auditor, and provides Pinnacle with the contractual right to exercise such audits; or
432: >
433: > \(iii\) At minimum, vendor requires each subprocessor to **provide SOC 2 Type II reports** and/or **ISO 27001 certifications** covering the relevant data processing services, with copies provided to Pinnacle upon request no less frequently than annually.
434: 
435: **Nice-to-have:** Pinnacle prefers the right to conduct **two (2) audits per calendar year**: one planned audit and one for-cause audit. Planned audits should require **fifteen (15) days\' prior written notice** to the vendor. For-cause audits, triggered by a breach, suspected breach, or other compliance concern, should require **no advance notice** to the vendor.
436: 
437: **Fallback:** One (1) planned audit per calendar year with **thirty (30) days\' prior written notice** is acceptable, provided that the following conditions are met:
438: 
439: > \(a\) For-cause audits are permitted **without notice** following a confirmed or suspected breach, a regulatory inquiry, or a material compliance concern identified by Pinnacle;
440: >
441: > \(b\) Audit scope extends to **all data processing locations**, including subprocessor sites, as described above;
442: >
443: > \(c\) Vendor provides **current SOC 2 Type II reports** and **ISO 27001 certifications** as a supplement to (not a replacement for) on-site audits, with reports and certifications provided to Pinnacle within thirty (30) days of request; and
444: >
445: > \(d\) Vendor cooperates fully with the audit, including by providing access to relevant personnel, documentation, and systems, and by making reasonable workspace available to Pinnacle\'s audit team during on-site audits.
446: 
447: **Red line:** Audit rights limited to a single vendor facility (excluding subprocessor sites) are **unacceptable**. Such a limitation would prevent Pinnacle from verifying compliance at the locations where data processing actually occurs, particularly where the vendor relies on subprocessors for hosting, storage, or processing activities. If vendor refuses to extend audit scope to subprocessor facilities, the negotiator must escalate immediately to Margaret Yuen-Park.
448: 
449: **[8.2 HIPAA Audit Requirements]{.underline}**
450: 
451: Under HIPAA, Pinnacle as Covered Entity must be able to audit Business Associates for compliance with the HIPAA Security Rule and Privacy Rule. The DPA/BAA must expressly state that Pinnacle\'s audit rights include the right to evaluate vendor\'s HIPAA compliance, including without limitation:
452: 
453: > • Review of vendor\'s HIPAA risk assessments (required under 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A));
454: >
455: > • Review of vendor\'s workforce training records and training content;
456: >
457: > • Review of vendor\'s security incident logs and breach response records;
458: >
459: > • Review of vendor\'s policies and procedures related to PHI access, use, disclosure, and safeguarding;
460: >
461: > • Interviews with vendor\'s HIPAA Privacy Officer and HIPAA Security Officer (or equivalents); and
462: >
463: > • Inspection of physical and technical safeguards at facilities where ePHI is created, received, maintained, or transmitted.
464: 
465: The HIPAA audit right must be independent of and in addition to any general audit right under the DPA. If the DPA\'s general audit provision is narrower than what HIPAA requires, the BAA must include a separate, broader audit provision that addresses the HIPAA-specific requirements listed above.
466: 
467: **[Section 9: Data Return, Deletion, and Retention]{.underline}**
468: 
469: This Section addresses the provisions governing the disposition of data at the end of the vendor relationship, including the critical interplay between post-termination data deletion obligations and HIPAA\'s six-year record retention requirement. Getting these provisions right is essential to ensuring both a clean transition and ongoing regulatory compliance.
470: 
471: **[9.1 Data Return Option]{.underline}**
472: 
473: **Must-have:** Upon termination or expiration of the DPA/MSA, for any reason, vendor must provide Pinnacle with a **data return option** --- that is, the right to receive a complete copy of all Personal Data, PHI, and California Personal Information processed by vendor under the DPA, in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format, before any deletion occurs. The data return option must be exercisable at Pinnacle\'s sole election; vendor may not condition the return of data on payment of additional fees beyond those specified in the DPA/MSA, nor may vendor require Pinnacle to waive any rights or claims as a condition of data return.
474: 
475: **Must-have:** Vendor must provide **at least thirty (30) calendar days of transition assistance** following Pinnacle\'s request for data return, during which period vendor must: (i) continue to securely host and maintain Pinnacle\'s data in accordance with all security and confidentiality obligations of the DPA; (ii) cooperate in data migration activities, including by making data available for export through secure channels and in agreed-upon formats; (iii) make relevant vendor personnel available to support the transition, including technical staff familiar with the data structures and systems involved; and (iv) refrain from deleting any Pinnacle data until Pinnacle has confirmed in writing that the data return is complete.
476: 
477: **Must-have:** Following completion of data return (or upon Pinnacle\'s written instruction to proceed directly to deletion without return), vendor must **securely delete all copies** of Pinnacle data in vendor\'s possession, custody, or control, including copies in active systems, staging environments, archives, and backup media. Pinnacle\'s playbook target is deletion within **thirty (30) calendar days** following completion of data return or receipt of Pinnacle\'s deletion instruction; the maximum acceptable deletion window is **sixty (60) calendar days**. Vendor must provide Pinnacle with a **written certification of deletion** signed by an authorized officer of vendor, confirming that all copies of Pinnacle data have been securely deleted using methods consistent with NIST SP 800-88 or equivalent standards.
478: 
479: **Nice-to-have:** Vendor provides data return in Pinnacle\'s preferred format (to be specified in the DPA or MSA), with all metadata intact and in a structure that facilitates import into Pinnacle\'s systems or a successor vendor\'s systems without material data loss or reformatting.
480: 
481: **Fallback:** If vendor insists on a longer deletion window (e.g., 90 days), this is acceptable only if: (i) the data return option is fully preserved; (ii) the 30-day transition assistance period is preserved; (iii) all security, confidentiality, and use restrictions of the DPA continue to apply to retained data throughout the extended deletion window; and (iv) vendor provides a written explanation of why 90 days is required (e.g., backup media rotation schedules).
482: 
483: **[9.2 HIPAA Record Retention]{.underline}**
484: 
485: **Must-have:** The DPA/BAA must acknowledge and account for HIPAA\'s **six (6) year record retention requirement** under 45 CFR § 164.530(j). Vendor must retain HIPAA-required documentation for six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when the document was last in effect, whichever is later. The categories of documentation subject to this requirement include:
486: 
487: > • The BAA itself;
488: >
489: > • Policies and procedures related to the privacy and security of PHI;
490: >
491: > • Workforce training records and training materials;
492: >
493: > • Security incident and breach response records;
494: >
495: > • Risk assessments and risk management documentation;
496: >
497: > • Access logs and audit trails related to PHI; and
498: >
499: > • Any other documentation required to demonstrate compliance with HIPAA requirements.
500: 
501: **Must-have:** The six-year HIPAA retention obligation must be **expressly reconciled** with the post-termination deletion obligation set forth in Section 9.1 above. Without an express reconciliation, the deletion obligation and the retention obligation create an internal contradiction that could result in either premature deletion of HIPAA-required records or indefinite retention of PHI without adequate contractual protections. Pinnacle\'s recommended reconciliation language is as follows:
502: 
503: > *\"Notwithstanding the deletion obligations in this Section, Processor shall retain such records as are required to comply with HIPAA record retention requirements (45 CFR § 164.530(j)) for a period of six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when such records were last in effect, whichever is later. Such retained records shall remain subject to the confidentiality, security, and use restrictions of this Agreement and the Business Associate Agreement for the duration of the retention period. Upon expiration of the applicable retention period, Processor shall securely delete all such retained records and provide Controller with written certification of deletion.\"*
504: 
505: **Red line:** Any post-termination deletion clause that does not carve out HIPAA record retention requirements is **non-compliant** and creates significant regulatory risk. A vendor that deletes HIPAA-required documentation within 30 or 60 days of termination may be in violation of 45 CFR § 164.530(j), and Pinnacle could face enforcement consequences if it cannot produce required documentation during an OCR investigation. Negotiators must ensure that the HIPAA retention carve-out is included in every DPA involving PHI. If a vendor\'s DPA template contains a blanket deletion-at-termination clause without a HIPAA carve-out, the clause must be redlined before execution. Escalate immediately if the vendor refuses to include the carve-out.
506: 
507: **[Section 10: Governing Law and Dispute Resolution]{.underline}**
508: 
509: Governing law and dispute resolution provisions are critical in DPAs that cover both US and EU data, particularly where the vendor is a non-US entity. A DPA that applies a single non-US governing law and non-US dispute resolution forum to all disputes --- including disputes involving US PHI and California personal information --- could undermine Pinnacle\'s ability to enforce its US regulatory rights and may be inconsistent with the jurisdictional framework of HIPAA and CCPA/CPRA enforcement. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s required approach: a bifurcated governing law and dispute resolution structure.
510: 
511: **[10.1 Bifurcated Governing Law]{.underline}**
512: 
513: **Must-have:** DPAs covering both US and EU data must include a **bifurcated governing law clause** that applies different governing law depending on the nature of the claim and the data involved:
514: 
515: > **(a) US Data Disputes.** All disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of **US data** --- including PHI, ePHI, CCPA/CPRA-covered personal information, and any other personal data of US-based data subjects --- shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the **State of Delaware**, without regard to its conflict of laws principles. Delaware law is Pinnacle\'s preferred governing law for US data disputes because Pinnacle is a Delaware corporation, Delaware has a well-developed body of commercial law, and the Delaware courts have extensive experience with complex commercial and data-related disputes.
516: >
517: > **(b) EU/EEA Data Disputes.** All disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of **EU/EEA data** --- including GDPR-covered personal data of EU/EEA data subjects --- shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the **applicable EU/EEA Member State**. Where Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V. is the contracting controller, the law of the **Netherlands** is preferred. Where the vendor is based in Germany and strongly resists Dutch law, **German law** is an acceptable alternative for EU data disputes.
518: 
519: **Nice-to-have:** Delaware law for all matters, including EU data disputes. However, this position is unlikely to be accepted by EU-based vendors and may conflict with GDPR mandatory provisions that require application of EU Member State law for certain data protection matters, including enforcement actions by supervisory authorities.
520: 
521: **Fallback:** German law for EU data disputes is acceptable, provided that Delaware law for US data disputes is preserved as a must-have. The bifurcation itself --- applying US law to US data disputes and EU law to EU data disputes --- is the critical structural requirement. Pinnacle will not accept a DPA that applies a single non-US governing law (e.g., German law) to disputes involving PHI or CCPA-covered personal information.
522: 
523: **[10.2 Dispute Resolution Forum]{.underline}**
524: 
525: **Must-have:** The DPA must include the following forum selection provisions:
526: 
527: > **(a) US Data Disputes.** The parties consent to the exclusive jurisdiction of the **United States District Court for the Western District of Texas, Austin Division**, or, where federal subject matter jurisdiction is unavailable, the **state courts of Travis County, Texas**, for all disputes arising from or related to the processing of US data. This forum selection reflects the location of Pinnacle\'s principal offices and the location of Pinnacle\'s primary US data processing operations.
528: >
529: > **(b) EU Data Disputes.** For disputes arising from or related to the processing of EU/EEA data, arbitration under recognized EU arbitration rules is acceptable. Pinnacle will accept arbitration administered by:
530: >
531: > • The **DIS** (Deutsche Institution für Schiedsgerichtsbarkeit / German Institution of Arbitration) Rules, seated in Germany;
532: >
533: > • The **ICC** (International Chamber of Commerce) Arbitration Rules, seated in the relevant EU jurisdiction; or
534: >
535: > • The **LCIA** (London Court of International Arbitration) Rules, seated in the relevant EU jurisdiction.
536: 
537: **Nice-to-have:** Federal court jurisdiction (Western District of Texas) for all disputes, including EU data disputes. This is unlikely to be accepted by EU vendors but should be proposed as the opening position.
538: 
539: **Fallback:** Pinnacle will accept arbitration for EU data disputes but will **NOT** accept non-US arbitration or non-US courts for disputes involving US data (PHI, CCPA-covered data, or any other US personal information). Any vendor DPA that applies a non-US governing law and/or a non-US dispute resolution forum to US data disputes must be **redlined**. Escalate to Margaret Yuen-Park and Rachel Osterfeld (Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP) if the vendor insists on a non-US forum for US data disputes.
540: 
541: **Note for negotiators:** Some vendor templates apply a single governing law (e.g., German law) and a single arbitration forum (e.g., Munich) to all disputes under the DPA, regardless of the type of data or the jurisdiction of the affected data subjects. This approach is problematic for several reasons:
542: 
543: > • HIPAA enforcement is under **US federal jurisdiction**. An arbitration clause seated in Munich may not be enforceable against an OCR subpoena or investigation, and may create practical barriers to Pinnacle\'s enforcement of its HIPAA-related contractual rights.
544: >
545: > • CCPA/CPRA enforcement is under **California jurisdiction** (California Attorney General and the California Privacy Protection Agency). A German arbitration clause may create uncertainty regarding the enforceability of CCPA-related contractual provisions.
546: >
547: > • A blanket non-US forum clause could undermine Pinnacle\'s ability to seek **injunctive relief** in US courts for urgent data protection matters, such as an ongoing unauthorized disclosure of PHI.
548: 
549: The bifurcated approach recommended in this Section addresses these concerns by ensuring that US data disputes are resolved in US forums under US law, while EU data disputes are resolved in EU forums under EU law.
550: 
551: **[Section 11: International Data Transfers]{.underline}**
552: 
553: While this playbook focuses primarily on US requirements, cross-border data transfers directly affect US data and must be addressed in vendor DPA negotiations. For example, EU data may be transferred to the US for disaster recovery or support purposes, and US data may be accessed remotely by vendor personnel located in the EU or other jurisdictions. The DPA must establish clear transfer mechanisms and documentation requirements for all such scenarios.
554: 
555: **[11.1 Transfer Mechanisms]{.underline}**
556: 
557: **Must-have:** Where vendor or any subprocessor transfers personal data from the EU/EEA to a third country (including the United States), the DPA must specify the applicable lawful transfer mechanism for each transfer scenario. Acceptable transfer mechanisms include:
558: 
559: > **(a) EU Standard Contractual Clauses (\"SCCs\")** adopted pursuant to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of 4 June 2021. The appropriate module must be selected for each transfer relationship:
560: >
561: > • **Module 2** (Controller-to-Processor): For transfers from Pinnacle EU B.V. (as Controller) to a vendor (as Processor) located outside the EEA;
562: >
563: > • **Module 3** (Processor-to-Subprocessor): For transfers from a vendor (as Processor) to a subprocessor located outside the EEA; and
564: >
565: > • **Module 4** (Processor-to-Controller): Where applicable, for reverse transfers.
566: >
567: > **(b) EU-US Data Privacy Framework (\"DPF\")** certification: Acceptable only if the receiving entity (vendor or subprocessor) is certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework and the certification covers the relevant data processing activities. Negotiators should verify the vendor\'s DPF certification status on the International Trade Administration\'s Data Privacy Framework List (dataprivacyframework.gov) before relying on this mechanism.
568: >
569: > **(c) Binding Corporate Rules (\"BCRs\")**: Acceptable where the vendor has approved BCRs in place that have been reviewed and approved by the competent EU supervisory authority.
570: 
571: **Must-have:** The DPA must address **all** transfer scenarios, including:
572: 
573: > • Primary data hosting and processing transfers (e.g., data stored in an EEA data center and processed by a US-based vendor);
574: >
575: > • Disaster recovery and business continuity transfers (e.g., data replicated to a US-based backup facility);
576: >
577: > • Remote access from third countries (e.g., vendor support engineers located in India, the Philippines, or the US accessing EU data from non-EEA locations); and
578: >
579: > • Subprocessor transfers (e.g., vendor engages a subprocessor in a third country to perform specific processing activities).
580: 
581: **Must-have:** Vendor must conduct and document a **Transfer Impact Assessment (\"TIA\")** for each transfer of personal data to a third country. The TIA must assess the laws and practices of the recipient country that may affect the protection of the transferred data, including government surveillance laws, and must be made available to Pinnacle upon request. Where the TIA identifies risks that cannot be mitigated by supplementary measures, the transfer mechanism may need to be reconsidered.
582: 
583: **Must-have:** If a subprocessor is not certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, SCCs must be executed with the appropriate module (typically Module 3, Processor-to-Subprocessor) before any personal data is transferred to that subprocessor.
584: 
585: **Nice-to-have:** Pinnacle pre-approves the specific SCC modules for each transfer relationship during DPA negotiation, ensuring clarity and reducing the need for post-execution amendments as transfer relationships evolve.
586: 
587: **Fallback:** If vendor\'s DPA template attaches only one SCC module (which is common), Pinnacle will require the addition of all applicable modules before execution. The negotiator should assess the vendor\'s transfer relationships and subprocessor arrangements to determine which modules are required and ensure that they are included in the DPA as executed.
588: 
589: **[Section 12: Subprocessing Requirements]{.underline}**
590: 
591: Vendors frequently engage subprocessors to perform specific data processing activities on their behalf. Because Pinnacle\'s data may ultimately be processed by entities with which Pinnacle has no direct contractual relationship, the DPA must include robust subprocessor requirements that ensure end-to-end protection. This Section works in conjunction with Section 8 (Audit Rights --- subprocessor coverage) and Section 4 (HIPAA BAA --- subcontractor flow-down).
592: 
593: **[12.1 Subprocessor Obligations]{.underline}**
594: 
595: **Must-have:** Vendor must impose on each subprocessor **substantially the same** data protection obligations as those imposed on vendor under the DPA. This flow-down requirement applies to all applicable regulatory regimes, including:
596: 
597: > • **HIPAA BAA flow-down terms**: Each subprocessor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI must be bound by BAA obligations equivalent to those in vendor\'s BAA with Pinnacle (per 45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii));
598: >
599: > • **CCPA/CPRA Service Provider restrictions**: Each subprocessor that processes California personal information must be contractually restricted from selling, sharing, combining, or using the personal information for purposes other than those specified in the agreement;
600: >
601: > • **GDPR Article 28 requirements**: Each subprocessor must be bound by a written contract that provides the same level of data protection as the vendor\'s DPA with Pinnacle (per GDPR Art. 28(4)); and
602: >
603: > • **Confidentiality obligations**: Each subprocessor must be bound by confidentiality obligations at least as protective as those in the DPA.
604: 
605: **Must-have:** Vendor remains **fully liable** for the acts and omissions of its subprocessors. The DPA must include an express statement that vendor shall be responsible for the performance of its subprocessors as if such acts or omissions were vendor\'s own. The use of subprocessors does not relieve vendor of any of its obligations under the DPA.
606: 
607: **Must-have:** The DPA must include a **current list of all authorized subprocessors**, specifying for each subprocessor:
608: 
609: > • Name and corporate entity;
610: >
611: > • Location (country and, where relevant, specific data center location);
612: >
613: > • Services provided to vendor in connection with Pinnacle\'s data; and
614: >
615: > • Description of the data processing activities performed by the subprocessor.
616: 
617: This list must be appended to the DPA as an exhibit or schedule and must be updated whenever a subprocessor is added, removed, or changed.
618: 
619: **Must-have:** Pinnacle (as Controller) must be notified of any proposed new subprocessor or change to existing subprocessors with **sufficient time to assess and object** to the change before it becomes effective. The DPA must provide Pinnacle with a meaningful objection right --- that is, the right to object to a proposed subprocessor and, if the objection is not resolved, the right to terminate the DPA without penalty.
620: 
621: **Nice-to-have:** A **thirty (30) day objection window** for new subprocessors, measured from the date of vendor\'s notification to Pinnacle. This provides Pinnacle with adequate time to assess the proposed subprocessor\'s data protection capabilities, conduct due diligence, and raise any concerns before the subprocessor begins processing Pinnacle\'s data.
622: 
623: **Fallback:** An objection window of **fourteen (14) to fifteen (15) calendar days** is acceptable and is consistent with current market norms for DPA negotiations. However, the objection window must not be shorter than fourteen (14) days, and the notification must include sufficient detail about the proposed subprocessor (including the information listed above) to enable Pinnacle to make an informed assessment.
624: 
625: **[Section 13: Security Requirements]{.underline}**
626: 
627: This Section sets forth the minimum security standards that must appear in every Pinnacle vendor DPA. These requirements apply to all vendors that process Pinnacle\'s data, regardless of the regulatory regime applicable to the data.
628: 
629: **[13.1 Technical and Organizational Measures]{.underline}**
630: 
631: **Must-have:** The DPA must reference and incorporate the following security frameworks:
632: 
633: > **(a) GDPR Article 32** --- Vendor must implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, the costs of implementation, and the nature, scope, context, and purposes of processing, as well as the risk of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms of natural persons. This reference is required for all DPAs involving EU/EEA data and is good practice for all DPAs.
634: >
635: > **(b) HIPAA Security Rule categories** --- Where vendor is a Business Associate, the DPA/BAA must require implementation of:
636: >
637: > • **Administrative safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.308, including security management processes, assigned security responsibility, workforce security, information access management, security awareness and training, security incident procedures, contingency planning, evaluation, and business associate contracts;
638: >
639: > • **Physical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.310, including facility access controls, workstation use, workstation security, and device and media controls; and
640: >
641: > • **Technical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.312, including access controls, audit controls, integrity mechanisms, person or entity authentication, and transmission security.
642: >
643: > Both the GDPR and HIPAA security frameworks must be explicitly referenced in the DPA. A DPA that references only GDPR Article 32 without addressing the HIPAA Security Rule is insufficient for vendors that process PHI.
644: 
645: **Must-have:** The DPA must require the following specific security measures:
646: 
647: > • **Encryption at rest**: Minimum AES-256 encryption for all Pinnacle data at rest, including data stored on servers, databases, storage arrays, and backup media;
648: >
649: > • **Encryption in transit**: Minimum TLS 1.2 for all data in transit, with **TLS 1.3 preferred**. Use of deprecated protocols (SSL, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1) is prohibited;
650: >
651: > • **Access controls**: Role-based access controls (\"RBAC\") based on the principle of least privilege, ensuring that only authorized personnel with a legitimate business need may access Pinnacle\'s data. Access must be reviewed and recertified at least quarterly;
652: >
653: > • **Multi-factor authentication**: Required for all remote access to systems containing Pinnacle data and for all administrative or privileged access.
654: 
655: **Must-have:** Vendor must hold a current **ISO 27001 certification** or equivalent information security management system certification, and must provide **SOC 2 Type II reports** covering the relevant service at least annually. Reports and certifications must be provided to Pinnacle within thirty (30) days of request.
656: 
657: **Nice-to-have:** Annual **penetration testing** conducted by a qualified third-party firm, with a summary of findings and remediation activities provided to Pinnacle. This is market standard and should be readily achievable by any vendor with a mature security program. Vendor should also agree to implement additional security measures as reasonably requested by Pinnacle to address evolving threats, emerging vulnerabilities, or changes in applicable law or regulatory guidance.
658: 
659: **[Section 14: Data Subject / Consumer Rights Assistance]{.underline}**
660: 
661: Pinnacle has obligations under HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR to respond to requests from individuals (patients, consumers, and data subjects) exercising their data protection rights. Because vendors often hold or process the data necessary to respond to these requests, vendor cooperation is essential. This Section sets forth the requirements for vendor assistance with data subject and consumer rights requests.
662: 
663: **Must-have:** Vendor must assist Pinnacle in responding to data subject and consumer rights requests under all applicable regulatory regimes, including but not limited to:
664: 
665: > **HIPAA --- Individual Access Rights.** Under 45 CFR § 164.524, individuals have the right to access their PHI. Pinnacle must provide access within **thirty (30) days** of the request, with one **thirty (30) day extension** permitted upon written notice to the individual. Vendor must cooperate with Pinnacle to identify, locate, and produce the requested PHI within a timeframe that enables Pinnacle to meet this regulatory deadline.
666: >
667: > **CCPA/CPRA --- Consumer Rights.** Under the CCPA/CPRA, California consumers have the right to know (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.110), the right to delete (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.105), the right to correct (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.106), the right to opt-out of sale/sharing (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.120), and the right to limit use of sensitive personal information (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.121). Pinnacle must respond to consumer requests within **forty-five (45) days**, with a **forty-five (45) day extension** upon notice to the consumer. Vendor must assist Pinnacle in fulfilling these requests, including by searching vendor\'s systems for the consumer\'s personal information, executing deletion or correction instructions, and confirming completion.
668: >
669: > **GDPR --- Data Subject Rights.** Under the GDPR, data subjects have the right of access (Art. 15), the right to rectification (Art. 16), the right to erasure (Art. 17), the right to restriction of processing (Art. 18), the right to data portability (Art. 20), and the right to object (Art. 21). Pinnacle/Pinnacle EU B.V. must respond to data subject requests within **thirty (30) days** per GDPR Art. 12(3), with a possible extension of two additional months for complex or numerous requests. Vendor must assist Pinnacle in responding within this timeframe.
670: 
671: **Must-have:** Vendor\'s assistance timeline must be **short enough** to allow Pinnacle to meet its own regulatory deadlines. Given the regulatory timelines above, vendor delay in responding to Pinnacle\'s requests for assistance could result in Pinnacle missing a statutory deadline, with potential enforcement consequences.
672: 
673: **Nice-to-have:** Vendor responds to Pinnacle\'s data subject/consumer rights assistance requests within **five (5) business days** of receipt. This provides Pinnacle with a meaningful buffer before its own regulatory deadlines expire.
674: 
675: **Fallback:** A response timeline of **ten (10) business days** is acceptable, provided that vendor commits to best efforts to respond sooner where Pinnacle indicates that the request is time-sensitive.
676: 
677: **[Section 15: DPA Term, Survival, and Termination Provisions]{.underline}**
678: 
679: This Section addresses the DPA\'s term, its relationship to the underlying MSA, and the critical question of which provisions survive termination and for how long.
680: 
681: **Must-have:** The DPA should be **coterminous with the MSA**. The DPA should become effective upon execution of the MSA (or, if later, upon the date the vendor first processes Pinnacle data) and should remain in effect until the MSA terminates or expires, unless terminated earlier in accordance with its terms. If the MSA is renewed or extended, the DPA should automatically renew or extend for the same period.
682: 
683: **Must-have:** The following DPA provisions must **survive termination** of the DPA and the MSA for a period sufficient to cover all applicable regulatory obligations:
684: 
685: > • **Breach notification** obligations (Section 5);
686: >
687: > • **Data return and deletion** obligations (Section 9);
688: >
689: > • **Liability and indemnification** obligations (Section 6);
690: >
691: > • **Audit rights** (Section 8), to the extent necessary to verify compliance with post-termination obligations;
692: >
693: > • **Confidentiality** obligations, for as long as vendor retains any Pinnacle data; and
694: >
695: > • **HIPAA BAA obligations**, for as long as vendor retains any PHI, and in any event for the six (6) year record retention period under 45 CFR § 164.530(j).
696: 
697: **Note on HIPAA Survival:** HIPAA requires six (6) years of record retention under 45 CFR § 164.530(j). Any DPA survival period shorter than six (6) years may be insufficient for HIPAA purposes, because the termination of the DPA\'s protective provisions before the end of the retention period would leave PHI-related documentation without contractual protections. Where a vendor proposes a shorter survival period (e.g., two (2) years), Pinnacle must negotiate either:
698: 
699: > \(a\) An extension of the general DPA survival period to six (6) years; or
700: >
701: > \(b\) A carve-out providing that HIPAA-related obligations (including the BAA, security obligations, audit rights, and confidentiality obligations as they relate to PHI) survive for the full **six (6) year retention period** or for as long as vendor retains any PHI, whichever is longer, even if the general DPA survival period is shorter.
702: 
703: **Fallback:** A general DPA survival period of **two (2) to three (3) years** is acceptable for non-HIPAA obligations, provided that HIPAA obligations have a separate, longer survival as described above. The negotiator should ensure that the survival clause clearly distinguishes between the general survival period and the HIPAA-specific survival period, and that the HIPAA survival is not inadvertently overridden by the general survival provision.

776: 
777: The following sample clause language is provided for use by Pinnacle negotiators when redlining vendor DPA templates.
